Flooding Disrupts Chemicals Industry Operations in Costa Rica

Flooding brought on by days of torrential rain in Costa Rica’s Caribbean region is causing significant disruption to the country’s chemicals industry, with several major sites and transport routes affected. The events began over the weekend, and emergency officials say the situation remains critical, with water levels still rising in parts of Limón and Matina.

Empaques Universal SA is among the companies reporting operational difficulties. The company’s packaging facility near Siquirres has been forced to halt production after access roads were flooded, preventing deliveries of raw materials and shipments of finished goods. “Our teams are working around the clock to assess damage and restore supply chains, but right now safety is our highest priority,” said company spokesperson Andrea Brenes. “We are in close contact with local authorities and hope to resume operations as soon as the roads are passable.”

Other chemicals producers in the area, including fertilizer and industrial solvent manufacturers, have also been impacted. According to the Costa Rican Chamber of Chemical Producers, at least four plants are operating at reduced capacity due to flooding of warehouses and transport delays. Riverbanks near key highways such as Route 32 have overflowed, hindering truck traffic essential for moving both inputs and finished chemical products to ports and customers.  

“The chemicals industry relies heavily on uninterrupted logistics,” explained industry analyst Mauricio Hidalgo. “With flooding affecting both production sites and transport routes, companies face mounting backlogs and risk breaching supply contracts.”

Authorities have not given an estimate for when water levels are expected to recede, citing ongoing rainfall forecasts. The National Emergency Commission has urged companies and residents to remain vigilant. “We are monitoring the situation closely and coordinating with industry contacts to ensure safety and facilitate recovery as soon as conditions allow,” said commission official Laura Pineda.

For now, chemicals industry leaders are bracing for continued disruption, with the full economic impact still unclear as the floodwaters persist.
